cues.text: Welcome to D and F Block Chemistry.
This recorded class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Begin with the configuration of the actual species.
Neutral chromium is commonly described as an argon core followed by three d
five and four s one.
Neutral copper has three d ten and four s one beyond that core.
These observed configurations are not replaced by an inflexible filling
shortcut.
For common first row metal cations, remove outer four s electrons before three
d electrons.
Neutral iron has three d six and four s two.
Removing two electrons gives iron two plus with a d six count; removing one
more gives iron three plus with d five.
Copper two plus has d nine, while zinc two plus has d ten.
A transition element has an incomplete d subshell in its atom or an important
cation.
Zinc's common atom and zinc two plus both have a filled d subshell, so a
position in the d block does not automatically make it a typical transition
element under that definition.
Outer s and d orbitals in transition elements can have relatively close
energies.
Different numbers of electrons can therefore participate in bonding,
supporting
several oxidation states.
Their relative stability depends on the element, ligands and medium.
Manganese in permanganate has formal oxidation state plus seven, but that does
not describe an ordinary free aqueous manganese seven plus ion.
The oxygen containing species and its bonding are essential.
High oxidation states are often stabilized with oxygen or fluorine, while many
later first row compounds favour lower states such as plus two or plus three.
Atomic radii also vary less dramatically across much of the transition series
than a simple main group comparison might suggest, because increasing nuclear
attraction and added d electrons compete.
Melting point and ionization trends contain exceptions and should be checked
against supplied data.
Separate a neutral metal, a dissolved ion and a solid oxide when explaining a
property.
Sharing the same elemental name does not make those species electronically or
structurally identical.
In an elementary magnetic model, unpaired electrons give paramagnetism, while
an all paired arrangement is diamagnetic.
The spin only moment estimate is the square root of the product of n and the
quantity n plus two, in Bohr magnetons, where n is the number of unpaired
electrons.
It is not simply the total d electron count.
A specified high spin d five arrangement has five unpaired electrons, so the
estimate is the square root of thirty five, about five point nine two Bohr
magnetons.
Other configurations require the actual orbital arrangement before counting n.
Ligand field strength can change the number of unpaired electrons for some d
counts, so oxidation state alone is not enough to predict every complex.
Orbital contributions and interactions can also make measured moments differ
from the spin only estimate.
Follow a clear sequence: identify the species, find the oxidation state and d
count, use the specified spin environment, then count unpaired electrons.
Only after those choices should the numerical formula be applied.
Many transition compounds absorb visible light through electronic transitions.
Splitting of d orbital energies in a ligand environment can allow d to d
absorption, but that is not the only mechanism.
Charge transfer transitions can give strong colours even when the metal is
formally d zero.
Permanganate is a familiar coloured example with manganese in oxidation state
plus seven and a formal d zero count.
A rule that every d zero compound must be colourless therefore fails.
Do not infer an exact colour from oxidation state alone: the ligands,
structure
and allowed transitions matter.
Transition metals and their compounds can also act as catalysts through
accessible oxidation states, reactive surfaces or intermediate complexes.
Small charged metal ions can accept electron pairs from donor ligands and form
coordination compounds.
These are broad explanations, not guarantees that every metal salt is a useful
catalyst.
A catalyst changes the reaction pathway and rate under suitable conditions,
while the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature remains a thermodynamic
property of the reaction.
Many transition metals are dense, strong solids with useful melting points,
although the pattern has exceptions.
Metallic bonding and the solid structure should be distinguished from the
behaviour of a dissolved metal salt.
Similar atomic sizes can help different metals occupy a common metallic
lattice
and form alloys.
An alloy need not be a pure molecular compound with one fixed stoichiometric
formula.
Its properties depend on the elements present, their proportions and the
resulting phases.
Small atoms such as carbon or nitrogen can occupy spaces in some metal
lattices, producing interstitial compounds or related solid phases.
These may retain metallic characteristics while becoming harder or showing
changed melting behaviour.
That does not make an interstitial solid a coordination complex in solution.
The same transition element can participate in several kinds of material, with
different structures and properties.
In a comparison question, identify whether it concerns the elemental metal, an
alloy, an interstitial solid or a salt before applying a general statement
about transition element chemistry.
In suitable acidic medium, permanganate is reduced to manganese two plus by
accepting five electrons per ion.
Dichromate is reduced to two chromium three plus ions by accepting six
electrons per dichromate ion.
These changes determine redox mole ratios.
Permanganate can give other manganese products in other media, so the five
electron factor is not universal.
Always read the medium and stated reduction product.
Preparation of potassium permanganate is conceptually connected with forming
manganate and then converting it to permanganate.
Potassium dichromate is connected with conversion of chromium ore to chromate
followed by the chromate dichromate relationship.
Acid base conditions shift that equilibrium: acid favours dichromate relative
to chromate under the usual comparison, while alkaline conditions favour
chromate.
This equilibrium changes the predominant species without itself changing
chromium's plus six oxidation state.
Distinguish acid base interconversion from reduction to chromium three plus.
The two processes use different bookkeeping even though the same element
appears in each.
Later examples will check both the electron and mole balances explicitly.
Lanthanoids involve progressive filling of four f orbitals, with plus three a
common oxidation state and important exceptions.
Across a comparable series of their trivalent ions, size generally decreases
because the increasing nuclear charge is not fully screened by added f
electrons.
This lanthanoid contraction contributes to the chemical similarity of
neighbouring members and can make their separation difficult.
Similar charge and gradually changing radius support similar behaviour, but do
not make every compound identical.
Contraction also helps explain the unexpectedly close sizes of some heavier
transition pairs, such as zirconium and hafnium.
Actinoids involve five f electrons and often show a wider range of accessible
oxidation states.
Their configurations and bonding require element specific treatment rather
than
a universal plus three label.
When comparing radii, use the same charge and a consistent radius definition;
changing both the oxidation state and element at once can obscure the trend.
The shielding explanation is a useful cause for a systematic comparison, not
permission to ignore the actual species in a table.
For a metal ion question, begin with the actual species and its oxidation
state.
Use the neutral configuration as the starting inventory, then remove the
appropriate outer electrons to obtain the ion.
For common first row cations, removing four s electrons before three d avoids
a
frequent counting error.
Next identify the ligand environment and any specified spin arrangement.
The same d count can lead to different magnetic behaviour in different
complexes.
For redox questions, specify the medium and the final oxidation state before
assigning an electron factor.
Balance atoms and total charge independently rather than accepting an equation
because the coefficients look familiar.
For trends, distinguish the first transition series from lanthanoids and
actinoids, and identify whether a value belongs to an atom, ion or solid.
A tabulated radius or magnetic moment needs its stated definition and
conditions.
Finally compare the result with basic limits: electron counts must match
charge, reaction charge must balance and a spin only unpaired count must fit
the available orbitals.
Consider iron two plus in a specified high spin d six arrangement.
Five d orbitals first receive one electron each, and the sixth makes one pair.
Four electrons remain unpaired.
The spin only estimate is the square root of four times six, or the square
root
of twenty four, about four point nine zero Bohr magnetons.
High spin iron three plus has d five with five unpaired electrons, giving
about
five point nine two.
In the elementary d nine arrangement for copper two plus, four orbitals are
paired and one has an unpaired electron.
The estimate is the square root of three, about one point seven three Bohr
magnetons.
These are model estimates, not exact measured values guaranteed for every
solid
or complex.
If the problem changes ligand field strength, check whether the assumed high
spin arrangement remains appropriate before reusing the result.
The total d count, the number of unpaired electrons and the numerical moment
are three different quantities that should be written separately.
Dichromate contains two chromium atoms, each at plus six.
Reducing both to plus three requires three electrons per chromium, giving six
per dichromate ion.
Iron two plus supplies one electron when it becomes iron three plus.
Therefore zero point zero one zero zero mole of dichromate can oxidize zero
point zero six zero zero mole of iron two plus under the stated acidic
reaction.
Permanganate becoming manganese two plus instead accepts five electrons per
ion.
Zero point zero two zero zero mole can therefore oxidize zero point one zero
zero mole of iron two plus.
Check charge as well as the mole ratio.
In the acidic permanganate half equation, minus one plus eight minus five
equals plus two, matching the product charge.
For dichromate, minus two plus fourteen minus six equals plus six, matching
two
chromium three plus ions.
Water and hydrogen ions must also balance oxygen and hydrogen atoms.
These checks distinguish a correct acidic equation from a memorized electron
factor used with the wrong product or medium.
Preparation equations become easier to understand when oxidation numbers are
checked alongside atom balance.
Chromite has formula iron chromium two oxygen four, with iron two and chromium
three in the elementary oxidation state description.
In the stated oxidative carbonate conversion, chromium becomes plus six in
chromate while iron becomes plus three in iron oxide.
The balanced equation uses four chromite units, eight sodium carbonate units
and seven oxygen molecules, giving eight sodium chromate, two iron oxide and
eight carbon dioxide units.
Eight chromium atoms each lose three electrons, while four iron atoms each
lose
one, making twenty eight electrons transferred.
Seven oxygen molecules accept that total when oxygen changes from zero to
minus
two.
Carbon remains plus four, so carbonate is not the redox donor merely because
carbon dioxide appears.
The sodium chromate product supplies the chromium containing intermediate for
subsequent dichromate chemistry.
Check chromium, iron, sodium, carbon and oxygen independently before deciding
coefficients.
These equations summarize chemical principles and the relationship between ore
and product, rather than specifying an operational preparation method or
claiming that the solid mixture behaves as a simple aqueous ionic reaction.
Chromate and dichromate provide a useful distinction between acid base
equilibrium and oxidation reduction.
Their interconversion can be written as two chromate ions plus two hydrogen
ions giving one dichromate ion and water, with a reversible arrow.
Chromium remains in oxidation state plus six on both sides.
Acidification therefore changes the balance between these species without
requiring electrons in the net equation.
In the common qualitative comparison, chromate is yellow and dichromate
orange.
Increasing hydroxide concentration consumes hydrogen ions and favours chromate
within the stated equilibrium conditions.
A basic form of the reverse conversion uses one dichromate plus two hydroxides
to give two chromates and one water.
Charge is minus four on each side of that equation.
The preparation of potassium dichromate can exploit the lower solubility of
its
salt relative to the corresponding sodium salt under the specified
crystallization conditions; it is not explained by changing chromium's
oxidation number during salt exchange.
Actual speciation depends on concentration and acidity, so the two ion
equation
is an organizing model rather than a claim that every chromium six solution
contains only one species of a single colour.
Manganate and permanganate differ by one unit of ionic charge and one unit of
manganese oxidation state.
The green manganate ion has manganese plus six, while the purple permanganate
ion has manganese plus seven.
In the usual preparation scheme, manganese dioxide is first converted under
alkaline oxidizing conditions to manganate.
An electrolytic oxidation can then remove one electron per manganate to form
permanganate.
The oxidation half equation is manganate giving permanganate plus an electron;
oxygen atom count is unchanged.
Manganate can also undergo disproportionation under suitable less strongly
basic conditions.
The balanced acidic representation uses three manganate ions and four hydrogen
ions to form two permanganate ions, one manganese dioxide and two waters.
Two manganese centres rise from six to seven, losing two electrons in total,
while one falls from six to four and gains two.
This is not simply a colour change caused by dilution.
State the chemical conditions and distinguish oxidation of all manganate from
simultaneous oxidation and reduction of different manganese centres.
These are reaction relationships for interpreting preparation chemistry, not a
laboratory recipe or a claim that every solution follows the same pathway
regardless of p H.
The electron factor of permanganate is not one fixed number independent of the
product.
In the familiar sufficiently acidic reduction to manganese two, manganese
changes from plus seven to plus two and accepts five electrons.
A balanced acidic half equation also consumes eight hydrogen ions and forms
four waters.
When the specified reduction product is manganese dioxide, manganese ends at
plus four and accepts three electrons.
A basic half equation uses permanganate, two waters and three electrons to
form
manganese dioxide and four hydroxides.
When the stated strongly alkaline comparison gives manganate, manganese ends
at
plus six and accepts one electron, with the same four oxygen atoms.
For one millimole permanganate, those three product assumptions correspond to
five, three or one millimole electrons.
Consequently an equivalent mass or a titration ratio must refer to the actual
product and reaction conditions.
Medium influences products, but the reducing agent, concentration and kinetics
also matter; a p H label alone does not guarantee the same outcome for every
reaction.
Balance atoms and total charge after selecting the stated product instead of
memorizing an electron factor without its chemical context.
Selected lanthanoid oxidation states become clearer when the actual ion
configuration is written.
Cerium three has one electron in the four f subshell in the usual ionic
description, while cerium four has an empty four f subshell.
Europium three has six four f electrons, and europium two has seven, giving a
half filled four f set.
Ytterbium three has thirteen four f electrons, while ytterbium two has
fourteen
and a filled set.
A four f subshell contains seven spatial orbitals and at most fourteen
electrons.
In the elementary Hund filling picture, the half filled seven electron set has
one electron in each orbital, whereas the fourteen electron set has all seven
pairs.
Empty, half filled or filled arrangements can help rationalize particular
oxidation state patterns, but electronic bookkeeping alone does not determine
stability in every chemical environment.
Lattice, hydration and redox energies also contribute.
Do not assume that the common plus three state gives the same f count for
every
element or that every lanthanoid readily exhibits all these alternatives.
The purpose of the comparison is to connect element identity, ionic charge and
occupancy before discussing periodic trends or magnetic evidence.
Actinoid configurations require specifying the actual species rather than
copying a neutral atom label onto every ion.
Use the supplied elementary neutral uranium configuration with a radon core,
three five f electrons, one six d electron and two seven s electrons.
In the simple isolated ion bookkeeping used here, forming uranium four plus
removes four outer electrons: the two seven s electrons, the six d electron
and one five f electron.
The remaining count is five f two.
The corresponding formal six plus uranium count is five f zero in this model.
Now consider the uranyl ion, containing uranium and two oxygens, with overall
charge plus two.
Assigning each oxygen minus two makes uranium oxidation state plus six,
despite
the whole ion having charge plus two.
Formal oxidation states and actual molecular electron density are different
descriptions, so this does not claim that uranyl consists of a free bare
uranium six plus ion.
More detailed actinoid bonding includes covalency and closely spaced orbitals.
Read overall charge, ligand oxidation assignments and the specified electron
count model separately before reporting an f configuration.
Matching d electron counts do not guarantee matching redox behaviour.
Chromium two plus and manganese three plus both have a formal d four count,
yet
their supplied aqueous reduction potentials differ.
Use minus zero point four one volt for chromium three plus accepting one
electron to become chromium two plus, and plus one point five one volts for
manganese three plus accepting one electron to become manganese two plus.
Combining manganese reduction with chromium two plus oxidation gives manganese
three plus plus chromium two plus forming manganese two plus plus chromium
three plus.
The standard cell potential is one point five one minus minus zero point four
one, or plus one point nine two volts.
One electron is transferred per written reaction.
With supplied Faraday constant ninety six thousand four hundred eighty five
coulombs per mole, standard Gibbs energy change is approximately minus one
hundred eighty five kilojoules per mole of reaction.
The resulting d five manganese two plus and d three chromium three plus counts
help organize the comparison, but measured potentials include the full
specified chemical environment.
Complexation, concentration and p H can change an actual redox comparison.
A carbide formula can support a composition calculation without determining
every property of an alloy.
Cementite has the formula iron three carbide, with three iron atoms for each
carbon atom.
Using supplied atomic masses iron fifty six and carbon twelve gives formula
mass one hundred eighty grams per mole.
The carbon mass fraction is twelve divided by one hundred eighty, or about six
point six seven percent.
Thus one point eight zero grams of pure ideal cementite contains zero point
one
two zero gram carbon and one point six eight grams iron.
Now use a stipulated two component mass model containing ten percent cementite
and ninety percent pure iron.
Since the pure iron component contributes no carbon, overall carbon percentage
is one tenth of the cementite carbon percentage, about zero point six six
seven
percent.
This does not mean a real steel is always described by only those two
components or that hardness is a linear function of carbon fraction.
Microstructure, phase distribution and processing also matter.
Count formula units and mass fractions before connecting a composition to any
independently supplied materials property data.
Oxide acid base behaviour can vary across oxidation states of the same
transition element.
In the introductory chromium comparison, chromium two oxide is mainly basic,
chromium three oxide is amphoteric, and chromium six oxide is acidic.
Charge balance gives chromium oxidation states plus two in the monoxide, plus
three in the two chromium three oxygen formula, and plus six in the trioxide.
A simple acid reaction for the monoxide uses two hydrogen ions to give
chromium
two ions and water.
For chromium three oxide, six hydrogen ions give two chromium three ions and
three waters.
Amphoteric behaviour also requires reaction with suitable base conditions; its
products depend on the stated medium.
Chromium trioxide can react with two hydroxide ions to give a chromate ion and
water, with chromium remaining plus six.
This last equation is acid base conversion, not a chromium oxidation state
change.
The comparison illustrates a useful trend toward acidic oxides at higher
oxidation state, rather than a universal classification rule for every
transition metal compound.
Keep oxide formula, oxidation state, reaction medium and redox classification
as separate checks.
The stability of an oxidation state cannot be decided from its electron count
alone.
Copper one has a formal filled d shell, yet simple aqueous copper one can
disproportionate to copper two and copper metal under the usual comparison.
Suitable ligands or an insoluble solid can change the thermodynamic situation.
A useful example is the supplied net reaction between copper two ions and
iodide, forming copper one iodide solid and iodine.
Two copper two ions each gain one electron to become copper one.
Two iodide ions supply those electrons by forming one iodine molecule, while
two additional iodides become the counterions in the two copper iodide formula
units.
The balanced net equation therefore uses four iodides per two copper two ions.
For a stipulated complete conversion of zero point zero one zero zero mole
copper two, the copper iodide amount is zero point zero one zero zero mole and
iodine amount zero point zero zero five zero zero mole.
Precipitation helps stabilize the copper one product here.
This does not contradict its instability in an otherwise different aqueous
system.
Identify ligands, phases and the full reaction before ranking oxidation
states.
A colour observation can be connected to an energy gap when the absorption is
assigned to a specified electronic transition.
For an illustrative absorption wavelength of five hundred nanometres, use the
supplied product of Planck's constant and light speed, twelve hundred forty
electron volt nanometres.
Dividing by wavelength gives two point four eight electron volts per absorbed
photon.
With one electron volt per particle corresponding to ninety six point four
eight five kilojoules per mole, the corresponding transition energy is about
two hundred thirty nine kilojoules per mole of such transitions.
This is an energy difference, not the absolute energy of an orbital or a bond
dissociation enthalpy.
A ligand field can produce d orbital splittings, but not every coloured
transition metal compound obtains its colour only from d to d absorption.
Charge transfer can be important, including in formally d zero permanganate.
The colour observed also depends on transmitted or reflected wavelengths
rather
than being simply identical to the wavelength most strongly absorbed.
State the transition assignment before interpreting the calculation, and do
not
infer the number of unpaired electrons from this wavelength alone.
Lanthanoid contraction affects more than the numerical radius of an isolated
ion.
Across a comparable series of trivalent lanthanoid ions, increasing nuclear
charge is not fully screened by added four f electrons.
The ions generally contract.
In the usual qualitative hydroxide comparison, the basic character decreases
from lanthanum hydroxide toward lutetium hydroxide as the smaller cations have
greater polarizing influence and the bonding becomes less purely ionic.
This is not permission to assign every salt solution a p H from atomic number
alone; solubility, hydrolysis and other equilibria matter.
The same contraction also helps explain the close sizes of some four d and
five
d transition pairs.
For supplied comparable six coordinate radii of seventy two picometres for
zirconium four and seventy one for hafnium four, the difference is only one
picometre.
Comparing the same charge, coordination number and radius convention is
essential.
Similar radii help rationalize similar chemistry and difficult separation, but
do not mean the elements have equal atomic numbers, isotope masses or
identical
compounds.
Use the contraction as a physical explanation under matched definitions rather
than a universal equality rule.
A catalytic redox cycle shows how accessible metal oxidation states can
provide
an alternative reaction route.
In a simplified homogeneous iron cycle, peroxodisulfate oxidizes two iron two
ions to two iron three ions while forming two sulfate ions.
The iron three ions can then oxidize two iodides to one iodine molecule,
returning to iron two.
Add the two balanced equations and cancel both iron forms that appear on
opposite sides.
The net reaction is one peroxodisulfate plus two iodides giving two sulfates
and one iodine.
Iron two is consumed in one stage and regenerated in the other, so its absence
from the net equation does not mean it never participates.
The written stages are balanced redox bookkeeping and are not a claim that
each
is a single elementary collision.
Detailed mechanisms can involve additional intermediates.
A catalyst changes the accessible kinetic pathway, not the equilibrium
constant
of the fixed overall reaction at the same temperature.
More catalyst can affect rate under suitable conditions, but cannot be counted
as a net stoichiometric product or assumed to shift the thermodynamic
equilibrium.
An indirect assay needs the stoichiometry of both chemical stages.
In a stipulated quantitative acidic model, one dichromate accepts six
electrons
while becoming two chromium three ions.
Negative iodide ions, written I minus, provide those electrons and form three
iodine molecules per dichromate.
Each iodine equivalent then reacts with two thiosulfate ions to form two
iodide
ions and one tetrathionate ion.
Combining the amounts gives six thiosulfates per dichromate.
After complete iodine capture and blank correction, a twenty five millilitre
sample corresponds to twenty millilitres of zero point zero three zero zero
molar thiosulfate.
The thiosulfate inventory is six times ten to the minus four mole.
Divide by six: dichromate inventory is one times ten to the minus four mole.
Divide by sample volume zero point zero two five litre: dichromate
concentration is four times ten to the minus three mole per litre.
With excess negative I minus ions, iodine may be carried as triiodide; the
iodine equivalent electron ledger remains the same.
This is an indirect assay model, not permission to assume that direct
dichromate thiosulfate mixing has this sole product.
Iodine loss, side reactions and incompatible acidity would require method
controls.
A balanced permanganate oxalate equation predicts amounts without giving the
complete kinetic mechanism.
In the specified acidic endpoint, manganese falls from plus seven to plus two
and accepts five electrons per permanganate.
Each carbon in oxalate begins at plus three and ends at plus four in carbon
dioxide.
One oxalate therefore donates two electrons.
Balancing ten electron equivalents requires two permanganates and five
oxalates, with sixteen hydrogen ions giving two manganese two ions, ten carbon
dioxide molecules and eight waters.
For zero point zero zero two zero zero mole permanganate consumed through this
model, oxalate consumption is zero point zero zero five zero zero mole and
carbon dioxide production zero point zero one zero zero mole.
The reaction also has a classic autocatalytic feature: manganese two product
can promote the reaction through a more complicated pathway involving
intermediate manganese species under suitable acidic conditions.
An initial slow period can therefore be followed by acceleration, though
reactant depletion eventually matters.
Stoichiometric coefficients do not establish reaction orders, and the balanced
net equation is not a single elementary collision.
State the endpoint and medium before applying either the electron factor or a
kinetic interpretation.
Empty and half filled f configurations help organize lanthanoid chemistry but
cannot decide every reaction by themselves.
Use supplied compatible reduction data of plus one point six one volts for
cerium four accepting one electron to become cerium three, and minus zero
point
three five volt for europium three accepting one electron to become europium
two.
Combine cerium reduction with europium two oxidation.
The balanced reaction converts one cerium four plus one europium two into
cerium three plus europium three.
Its standard cell potential is one point nine six volts and the electron
transfer number one.
With Faraday constant ninety six thousand five hundred, the standard Gibbs
change is minus one hundred eighty nine point one four kilojoules per mole of
written reaction.
Cerium four begins with formal f zero and europium two with f seven, whereas
the products have f one and f six.
Thus a preference slogan about empty or half filled shells cannot override the
supplied redox thermodynamics.
Solvation, ligands and medium contribute to the measured potentials, and
actual
nonstandard mixtures require their reaction quotient.
Both sides have total ionic charge plus six, so charge and electrons remain
balanced without inventing a two electron transfer.
Transition metal density is a mass per volume property, not a direct count of
unpaired electrons.
A supporting data calculation uses density equal to molar mass divided by
molar
volume for the stated pure phase at its temperature and pressure.
With supplied rounded copper data, molar mass sixty three point five grams per
mole and molar volume seven point one zero cubic centimetres per mole, the
ratio is about eight point nine four grams per cubic centimetre.
The mole units cancel; this is not grams per mole again.
Comparing two metals requires both quantities.
In an original hypothetical pair, the second molar mass is one point five
times
the first, but its molar volume is twice as large.
Its density is therefore only three quarters of the first despite the heavier
atoms.
Across a transition series, changes in atomic volume and structure can shape
the observed pattern, so a simple increase in atomic number does not guarantee
monotonic density or melting point.
Alloy composition, phases and volume changes need their own information;
averaging component densities is not a general law.
Keep density, hardness, magnetism and bond strength as distinct properties.
Specifying an oxidant's reduction product does not remove its dependence on
acidity.
Reaction stoichiometry sets the pH coefficient.
Consider the acidic permanganate to manganese two half reaction at two hundred
ninety eight kelvin.
One permanganate consumes eight hydrogen ions and five electrons to form one
manganese two ion and four waters.
In a supplied ideal activity comparison, keep permanganate and manganese two
activities at one and take standard potential one point five one volt.
The reaction quotient then contains the reciprocal eighth power of hydrogen
ion
activity.
Applying the Nernst equation gives potential one point five one minus eight
times zero point zero five nine two divided by five, multiplied by pH.
Raising pH from zero to two lowers the predicted potential by about zero point
one eight nine four volt, giving about one point three two zero six volt.
This is a comparison of the same specified acidic half reaction.
It must not be extrapolated through every pH range while forcing manganese two
to remain the product.
Other manganese species, precipitation and activity effects can change the
relevant comparison.
A back titration measures the oxidant left over, not the oxidant consumed by
the sample.
Use a supplied ideal iron assay in which every sample iron atom has first been
converted to iron two, no other sample component reduces dichromate, and the
specified reactions go to completion.
One dichromate ion accepts six electrons in acid, while each iron two ion
loses
one electron.
An initial three millimoles of dichromate therefore offers eighteen millimoles
of electron accepting capacity.
After the sample reacts, the unused dichromate requires four millimoles of a
separate iron two standard in the back titration.
Those four millimoles measure residual oxidizing capacity and must be
subtracted from eighteen, leaving fourteen millimoles attributable to sample
iron.
Using rounded iron molar mass fifty six grams per mole gives zero point seven
eight four gram iron.
For a one gram sample, the ideal iron mass fraction is seventy eight point
four
percent.
The original dichromate amount cannot be treated as entirely consumed by the
sample.
Interfering reductants or incomplete conversion would invalidate the
stipulated
assay interpretation.
A measured effective magnetic moment of a mixture need not equal the moment of
any one isolated ion.
Use a supporting ideal Curie model with noninteracting high spin iron two and
iron three centers at the same temperature.
Assume orbital contributions and diamagnetism have been excluded and normalize
susceptibility per mole of total iron.
High spin iron two has four unpaired electrons, giving spin only moment
squared
four times six, or twenty four in squared Bohr magneton units.
High spin iron three has five, giving five times seven, or thirty five.
Susceptibility contributions add in proportion to these squared moments, so a
fraction f of iron three gives mixture moment squared twenty four plus eleven
f.
If the supplied corrected effective moment squared is thirty point six,
solving
gives f equal to zero point six, or sixty percent iron three.
The effective moment is about five point five three Bohr magnetons, but
averaging the two moment magnitudes directly is not the Curie mixture
calculation.
Real orbital contributions, magnetic interactions or different normalization
would require a different model.
An absorption wavelength gives an energy difference, while absorbance at a
fixed wavelength can provide concentration information under additional
assumptions.
In a supporting Beer Lambert model, absorbance equals molar absorptivity times
optical path length times concentration.
Use an illustrative diluted permanganate sample whose chemical form is
unchanged, with blank corrected absorbance zero point four zero zero, path
length one centimeter and supplied molar absorptivity two thousand liters
divided by moles and centimeters.
The measured concentration is zero point four divided by two thousand, giving
two times ten to the minus four molar.
If this sample was made by a fivefold dilution, the original concentration was
one times ten to the minus three molar.
Absorbance is dimensionless and is not the fraction of light absorbed.
Transmittance is ten to the power minus absorbance, about zero point three
nine
eight here, or thirty nine point eight percent transmission.
The model assumes an appropriate calibration range, fixed wavelength, clear
solution and no chemical change.
Scattering, stray light or changing manganese speciation can invalidate the
simple concentration inference.
